significance.justification: A verified-true result would license the form-(iii) predictive coupling that "high alignment (entanglement) between" self-truth and agent-attributed-belief directions predicts Theory-of-Mind errors, supplemented by the form-(ii) causal finding that steering or forcing this alignment selectively repairs or induces egocentric answers. This establishes both a behavioral phenomenon and a mechanism, constraining expected errors under changes in subspace alignment rather than merely showing that another agent's belief is decodable; that is material to the benchmark fragility highlighted by Ullman's 2023 "Large Language Models Fail on Trivial Alterations to Theory-of-Mind Tasks." The negative branch would rule out this geometric-entanglement account if attributed beliefs remain separable during errors and manipulating overlap does not affect behavior, although failure of one part of the claim's broad conjunction would be less decisive. In the topic-substitution check, generic research on LLM belief representations would not earn this score: the alignment-error coupling and independently manipulable self/other decomposition are the claim-specific reasons it exceeds the obvious probing hypothesis.

reach.justification: The named handles are "principal-angle separation" as a diagnostic quantity and the training-time "attribution-disentanglement regularizer" as an intervention; the latter is ex ante because it changes the model before false-belief answers are produced, while the per-example alignment analysis is mainly post hoc or concurrent. After per-model re-extraction, the conclusion predicts a transferable relation—greater self/other subspace overlap should accompany more egocentric errors—rather than merely supplying a procedure for rediscovering an unconstrained direction, though it gives no quantitative threshold or scaling law. The hypothesis is stated for LLMs and names multiple families while conceding that "results may vary across model families"; downstream users could include model trainers and auditors who use separation as a retention-aware training constraint, not only researchers explaining the errors. The topic-substitution check fails decisively: deleting the principal-angle predictor and regularizer leaves no comparable handle or practitioner action window, so the reach score comes from this claim rather than from the broad importance of LLM beliefs.
